evidence_items.locator: Section 1, Introduction; experimental details in sections 2.1–2.2 and appendix D.3
evidence_items.explanation: Before-and-after comparisons found increased expressed overconfidence after preference training. Reward experiments favored higher confidence for otherwise identical responses, while modified reward training reduced calibration error, supporting training as a contributing cause.

Elicited confidence can track correctness better than token probabilities, with results varying by model and prompt. This limits the stronger interpretation that confidence is always meaningless; it does not establish that ordinary confident wording guarantees accuracy.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; manuscript marked accepted to ACL 2026 Findings
evidence_items.explanation: Experiments across six open-weight models found that instruction tuning harmed calibration and chat formatting further increased confidence in models' own answers. This supports training as one cause while identifying an additional cause in how the interaction is presented.

unresolved_gaps: The experiments do not isolate the training causes of confident medical prose in every proprietary chatbot available when Marcus wrote.
The evidence establishes a contributing mechanism, not that all confidence is uninformative or that training is its sole cause.
